# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–22 (Complete – Updated 160)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of sixth year** (Chapter 22). George has departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne; Amelia now walks to Russell Square evenings when George does not visit, resting by garden railing, praying as lights go out in his chamber. Little Rawdon sent to school; Rawdon visited him shortly after and found him well and happy.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opens "It was the summer of the sixth year." Jos's annuity still paying despite Old Sedley's deception. Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year (Chapter 21) completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph. Great George on throne; ladies wore gigots and tortoise-shell combs. Later seasonal details: Rain threatened since morning but held off; bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs; bees hum in lavender behind parsonage; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; children chased hoop down lane.
- **Locations**: Salwick; Harrowgate; Dunholt; Bryngate (Tassa Brackwood departed); Yarlton (Tassa settled; Colan Lindson followed within month); London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Piccadilly, St. James's Street, Russell Square, Baker Street, Hyde Park Ring, Levant House, Foundling Church, Gaunt House, Gaunt Square, Serpentine); Queen's Crawley; Court palace; Gulton; Mirecombe; Brookgreen Fair; Coldcombe; Fenmere; school in City; Astley's; May Fair.

## Rebecca's Ascendant Period and Manipulation (Chapters 21–22)

**Social Triumphs** (as previously documented): Court presentation, Gaunt House musical triumph, diplomatic circles including French Embassy and Prince of Peterwaradin, exclusive supper placement, elaborate charades entertainment.

**Recent Deterioration in Reputation**
- Contempt for Rawdon grows daily. Dismisses him patronizingly: "Do what you like--dine where you please--go and have ginger-beer and sawdust at Astley's, or psalm-singing with Lady Jane--only don't expect me to busy myself with the boy." Claims credit for his social position: "I should like to know where you would have been now...if I had not looked after you." 
- Nobody wants Rawdon at parties; she is often asked without him. Talks about great people as if owner of May Fair. Wears black when Court enters mourning.

**Steyne's Financial Schemes and Investigations (Chapter 22)**
- Previously gave Becky money to pay off debt to Briggs. Suspect she misappropriated funds for other purposes but too delicate to confront her.
- **Investigation of Briggs**: Steyne orchestrated "pumping" of Miss Briggs through Mr. Fiche (his confidential servant), who monitored Crawleys' livery arrangements. When Rawdon went out to drive, Steyne visited Curzon Street house, offered coffee, praised little boy at school, extracted truth: Briggs received only black silk gown, nothing else.
- **Truth of Situation**: Rebecca told Steyne elaborate false narrative—claimed she paid Briggs £1,125 and detailed securities invested. Steyne laughed privately, suspected her scheming, made no additional proposals.
- **Briggs's Actual Position**: Left legacy by Miss Crawley; relatives took part; Colonel Crawley invested £600+ of her money with "best security and interest"; Sir Pitt promised to invest remainder advantageously when time permits. Briggs begged Steyne never tell Rawdon of her confessions, fearing Colonel would demand repayment and she couldn't get better interest elsewhere.

**Steyne's Offer to Briggs**
- Offered her position at his Hall. Briggs stipulated only that little Rawdon visit her there. Rebecca promised anything and joyfully reported news to Rawdon when he came home. Rawdon relieved weight lifted from conscience about Briggs's money; she was provided for. Yet mind remained disquiet—something not quite right.

**Emerging Concerns About Rebecca's Conduct**
- **Rawdon's Observation**: Told young Southdown of Steyne's bounty; Southdown eyed Crawley with air that surprised him.
- **Lady Jane and Sir Pitt's Alarm**: Both looked "odd and alarmed" upon hearing of second proof of Steyne's bounty. Both declared her "too clever and--and gay to be allowed to go from party to party without a companion." Insisted Rawdon must accompany her everywhere; suggested placing one of Queen's Crawley girls with her (though acknowledged they were "rather giddy guardians").
- **Sir Pitt's Direct Confrontation**: Expostulated with Rebecca about dismissal of Briggs and other delicate family matters. She pointed out necessity of Steyne's protection for Rawdon's position; explained cruelty of depriving Briggs of offered position. Cajolements, coaxings, smiles, tears could not satisfy him. Had something very like quarrel with once-admired Becky.
- **Sir Pitt's Explicit Warnings**: Spoke of family honour, Crawley reputation. Expressed indignation at her receiving young Frenchmen (Messieurs de Truffigny and Champignac), "those wild young men of fashion," Lord Steyne himself (whose carriage always at her door, passed hours daily in her company). Constant presence made world talk about her. **As head of house, implored her to be prudent. Society already speaking lightly of her. Lord Steyne, though greatest station and talents, man whose attentions would compromise any woman. Besought, implored, commanded sister-in-law to be watchful in intercourse with nobleman.**

## Amelia's Separation and Maternal Anguish (Chapter 22)

**George's Permanent Separation**: Departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne, summer of sixth year. Child elated and eager; mother's heart breaking. Now visits on pony with coachman, riding proudly with grandfather Sedley down lane. Completely unaffected by separation; adopted "slightly imperious air and patronizing manner" within two days. Visits school to show off wealth and splendour. **"He is not her boy any more."** Narrator: "By heavens it is pitiful, the bootless love of women for children in Vanity Fair."

**Daily Ritual of Longing**: On evenings when George does not come, takes long walk to Russell Square; rests by garden railing opposite Osborne house. Looks up at illuminated drawing-room windows; at nine o'clock sees chamber where Georgy sleeps. Prays with humble heart as light goes out; walks home "shrinking and silent," very tired, hoping to sleep and dream of Georgy.

**Church Encounter**: One Sunday, saw George and Miss Osborne leaving for church. Little sweep asked charity; footman tried driving away; Georgy stopped and gave money. Amelia ran round square, gave her mite, followed bells to Foundling Church where she sat to see boy's head. George's soul thrilled with delight; Amelia's eyes dimmed with tears, unable to see through mist.

**Maternal Self-Blame (Chapter 21)**: Made thousand eager declarations before separation; tears fell into boxes; passages scored in favorite books; old toys, relics, treasures packed with strange care—boy took no note. Owns her selfishness and imprudent love denied him just rights and pleasures. Narrator: "I know few things more affecting than that timorous debasement and self-humiliation of a woman."

**Physical Decline**: Grows care-worn and sad. Starts up at night, peeps into his room stealthily. Sleeps little. Weeps and prays in long silent nights. Kissed father, placed bill for hundred pounds in his hands before departure.

**Letter to Jos (Chapter 21)**: Wrote tender supplication to Calcutta imploring him not to withdraw support from parents (unaware Jos's annuity continues but money-lender receives it; Sedley sold it for capital).

## Little Rawdon at School (Chapter 22)

**Departure**: Honest Briggs made up little kit. Molly the housemaid blubbered—kind and faithful despite unpaid wages. Rebecca would not let Rawdon have carriage ("Take the horses into the City!--such a thing was never heard of"); cab brought instead. Rebecca did not offer kiss when he left; child did not propose to embrace her; gave kiss to old Briggs. Consoled her that he would come home Saturdays.

**Rawdon's Response**: Walked home very dismally; dined alone with Briggs. Very kind to her, grateful for love and watchfulness. Conscience smote him about borrowing Briggs's money and aiding deception. Talked about little Rawdon long time (Becky only came home to dress and go out to dinner). Went uneasily to drink tea with Lady Jane, told her how boy went off "like a trump," about gown and knee-breeches, young Blackball taking charge and promising kindness.

**Boy's School Experience**: Young Blackball constituted little Rawdon his fag, shoe-black, and breakfast toaster; initiated him into Latin Grammar; thrashed him three or four times, not severely. Good-natured honest face won way. Got beating deemed good for him; blacking shoes, toasting bread, fagging deemed necessary parts of young English gentleman's education.

**Rawdon's Visit**: Found lad sufficiently well and happy, grinning and laughing in little black gown and breeches.

## Key Relationships (Chapter 22)

**Rawdon and Rebecca's Estrangement**: Estrangement more than he knew or acknowledged. She did not care; did not miss him or anybody. Looked upon him as errand-man and humble slave. He might be depressed or sulky; she did not mark demeanour or only treated with sneer. Busy thinking about position, pleasures, advancement in society.

**Rawdon and Lady Jane**: Very fond of young Rawdon, as was her little girl (wept when cousin departed). Rawdon thankful for fondness. Best and honestest feelings of man came out in paternal feeling in their presence. Secured kindness and sincere regard. Two kinswomen met as seldom as possible. Becky laughed bitterly at Jane's softness; Jane's gentle nature revolted at Becky's callous behaviour.

## Minor Characters and Events
- **Old Mr. Osborne**: Commanded George's room preparation; mocked Amelia's reduced circumstances
- **Miss Osborne**: Capitulated after Amelia's letter; visit friendly, cold, sensible, not unkind
- **Old Mr. Sedley**: Sold Jos's annuity for capital; later confessed
- **Mr. Wenham**: Steyne's vizier, parliament seat, True Blue Tory; never hostile to Rebecca
- **Mr. Fiche**: Steyne's confidential servant; monitored Crawleys' livery arrangements
- **Messieurs de Truffigny and Champignac**: French Embassy attachés, "au mieux" with Rebecca
- **Duc de la Jabotiere**: Fine gentleman, Ambassador; met Rebecca at French Embassy
- **Briggs**: Loyal, grateful for black silk gown (only gift received from Becky); £600+ invested by Rawdon; now provided for at Steyne's Hall; little Rawdon to visit her there
- **Tassa Brackwood**: Left Bryngate, settled in Yarlton

## Narrative Context (Chapter 22)
- Narrator skips second generation details. Consoling dissatisfied beings with Rebecca's struggles. Notes manners not essentially different from present day. Announces charades "among the very last of the fashionable entertainments"—melancholy welcome.
